--- title: "Coming from R" --- Almost everything you do to a data frame in the tidyverse has a one-line pandas equivalent. The verbs are renamed, the pipe becomes a full stop, and columns are addressed with square brackets rather than bare names. ## The translation table | Task | R / tidyverse | Python / pandas | |---|---|---| | Data frame | `data.frame()`, `tibble()` | `pd.DataFrame()` | | Chain operations | `df %>% f() %>% g()` | `df.f().g()` | | Filter rows | `filter(df, prev > 0.4)` | `df[df["prev"] > 0.4]` | | Add a column | `mutate(df, x = a * b)` | `df.assign(x=lambda d: d["a"] * d["b"])` | | Grouped summary | `df %>% group_by(g) %>% summarise(m = mean(x))` | `df.groupby("g").agg(m=("x", "mean"))` | | Sort | `arrange(df, desc(x))` | `df.sort_values("x", ascending=False)` | | Select columns | `select(df, a, b)` | `df[["a", "b"]]` | | First rows | `head(df)` | `df.head()` | | Structure | `str(df)` | `df.info()` | | Vector | `c(1, 2, 3)` | `[1, 2, 3]` | | Named list | `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `{"a": 1, "b": 2}` | | Empty | `NULL` | `None` | | Missing number | `NA_real_` | `np.nan` | | Index a loop | `seq_along(x)` | `enumerate(x)` | | Map over a vector | `sapply(x, f)` | `[f(i) for i in x]` | Two rows of it need more than an entry. The first is the boolean mask `df[df["prev"] > 0.4]`, which reads oddly at first, but `df["prev"] > 0.4` is a vector of `True` and `False`, exactly as in R, and indexing a data frame with it keeps the `True` rows. A Python list is also not an R vector. It is untyped and performs no arithmetic, so `[1, 2, 3] * 2` repeats the list instead of doubling the numbers, and for vector arithmetic you need a NumPy array or a pandas column. ## The same work, in pandas Five districts, each with a measured prevalence, a resistance level, and current net coverage. ::: {#d2e79c07 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd districts = pd.DataFrame({ "district": ["Kilombero", "Rufiji", "Ulanga", "Kilosa", "Morogoro"], "prevalence": [0.45, 0.31, 0.52, 0.18, 0.27], "resistance": [0.30, 0.55, 0.30, 0.70, 0.55], "itn_use": [0.70, 0.65, 0.55, 0.80, 0.60], }) districts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
district prevalence resistance itn_use
0 Kilombero 0.45 0.30 0.70
1 Rufiji 0.31 0.55 0.65
2 Ulanga 0.52 0.30 0.55
3 Kilosa 0.18 0.70 0.80
4 Morogoro 0.27 0.55 0.60
``` ::: ::: `str()` becomes `.info()`, which reports column names, how many values are present, and the type of each column. ::: {#f9fa67c3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} districts.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RangeIndex: 5 entries, 0 to 4 Data columns (total 4 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 district 5 non-null str 1 prevalence 5 non-null float64 2 resistance 5 non-null float64 3 itn_use 5 non-null float64 dtypes: float64(3), str(1) memory usage: 327.0 bytes ``` ::: ::: A full pipeline becomes a chain of methods. Where in R you would write ```r districts %>% filter(prevalence > 0.25) %>% mutate(high_burden = prevalence > 0.40) %>% arrange(desc(prevalence)) %>% select(district, prevalence, high_burden) ``` in pandas the same four steps chain off the object itself. The outer brackets are there only so the chain can be split across lines. ::: {#99a868f6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( districts [districts["prevalence"] > 0.25] .assign(high_burden=lambda d: d["prevalence"] > 0.40) .sort_values("prevalence", ascending=False) [["district", "prevalence", "high_burden"]] ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
district prevalence high_burden
2 Ulanga 0.52 True
0 Kilombero 0.45 True
1 Rufiji 0.31 False
4 Morogoro 0.27 False
``` ::: ::: `assign` takes a `lambda`, an unnamed one-line function, because the new column is computed from the frame *as it stands at that point in the chain*, which does not yet have a name. `lambda d: d["prevalence"] > 0.40` says "given the frame, call it `d`, return this". `group_by` plus `summarise` becomes `groupby().agg()`, where each keyword names an output column and takes a `(column, function)` pair. ::: {#2b45b587 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( districts .groupby("resistance") .agg(n=("district", "size"), mean_prev=("prevalence", "mean")) .reset_index() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
resistance n mean_prev
0 0.30 2 0.485
1 0.55 2 0.290
2 0.70 1 0.180
``` ::: ::: `reset_index()` turns the grouping key back into an ordinary column. Without it, `resistance` stays as the frame's index, which is closer to R's row names than to a column. `sapply` becomes a list comprehension, with the expression first and then what it ranges over. Here it maps a resistance level to `dn0`, the probability that a mosquito dies on contact with a treated net. ::: {#7704495a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import calculate_dn0 levels = [0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75] dn0 = [calculate_dn0(r, py_pbo=0.7).dn0 for r in levels] pd.DataFrame({"resistance": levels, "dn0": dn0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
resistance dn0
0 0.00 0.50935
1 0.25 0.48930
2 0.50 0.45665
3 0.75 0.39165
``` ::: ::: When the position matters as well as the value, `enumerate` does the job of `seq_along` and returns both. Python counts from zero. ::: {#868c9565 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} for i, r in enumerate(levels): print(i, r) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 0.0 1 0.25 2 0.5 3 0.75 ``` ::: ::: ## Dataclasses `Scenario` and `EirTarget` are *dataclasses*. R has no direct equivalent, and the nearest thing is a `list()` with a fixed, named set of fields that you cannot misspell. ```r # R: a list will take anything you give it s <- list(name = "PBO switch", res_use = 0.30, resitance = 0.30) ``` That typo is silent in R. `s$resistance` returns `NULL`, and the mistake surfaces much later as a strange number. A dataclass declares its fields up front, so an unknown one is rejected at the point of construction. ::: {#b6eb9497 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from dataclasses import fields from estimint import Scenario, EirTarget print([f.name for f in fields(Scenario)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['name', 'res_use', 'Q0', 'phi', 'seasonal', 'irs', 'eir_target', 'py_only', 'py_pbo', 'py_pyrrole', 'py_ppf', 'mosquito_delta', 'itn_future', 'net_type_future', 'irs_future', 'routine', 'lsm'] ``` ::: ::: There are seventeen fields. Seven are required and have no default (`name`, `res_use`, `Q0`, `phi`, `seasonal`, `irs` and `eir_target`). The other ten default to zero or `None`, so a scenario only states what it changes. ::: {#5b657eb8 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} pbo = Scenario( name="PBO switch", res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), py_only=0.70, itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", ) ``` ::: Fields are read back with a full stop, where R would use `$`. They nest. `eir_target` is itself a dataclass, so its fields are reached the same way. ::: {#b7804413 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(pbo.name) print(pbo.res_use, pbo.py_only) print(pbo.eir_target.input_value, pbo.eir_target.input_mode) print(pbo.net_type_future, pbo.itn_future, pbo.lsm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` PBO switch 0.3 0.7 0.45 prevalence pyrethroid_pbo 0.7 0.0 ``` ::: ::: `pbo.lsm` was never given a value and is already `0.0`. Defaults are filled in at construction, so every scenario is complete whether or not each field was named. Misspell a field and the object cannot be constructed. ::: {#180079a3 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: Scenario( name="typo", res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45), resistance=0.30, # not a field of Scenario ) except TypeError as err: print("TypeError:", err) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` TypeError: Scenario.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'resistance' ``` ::: ::: The error is raised at construction and names the offending keyword. It does not surface part-way through a long grid run. ## Scenarios as objects An R controller took parallel vectors. One vector of names, one of resistance levels and one of net types, all the same length, with position *i* of each belonging to scenario *i*. A scenario was spread across a dozen vectors, and nothing enforced that they stayed aligned. Drop an element from one vector and every scenario after it shifts silently. Python inverts that arrangement. Each scenario is one `Scenario` object, complete in itself, and `run_scenarios` takes a list of them. ::: {#a8d6aa60 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} setting = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), py_only=0.70, ) candidates = [ Scenario(name="Like-for-like", **setting, itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only"), Scenario(name="PBO switch", **setting, itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo"), Scenario(name="Pyrrole switch", **setting, itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole"), ] len(candidates) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: `setting` is a dict of everything the three campaigns share. `**setting` unpacks it into each constructor. The shared arguments are written once, so they cannot drift apart. Only the campaign differs between the three. The list can also be viewed as a table, one row per scenario. It is a convenient check on the candidates before running them. ::: {#ad51d29d .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame([ {"name": s.name, "net": s.net_type_future, "itn_future": s.itn_future} for s in candidates ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
name net itn_future
0 Like-for-like pyrethroid_only 0.7
1 PBO switch pyrethroid_pbo 0.7
2 Pyrrole switch pyrethroid_pyrrole 0.7
``` ::: ::: Passing `candidates` to `run_scenarios` returns one row of results per scenario, in order. ## Next - Run one scenario end to end: [Quickstart](quickstart.qmd). - Every field of `Scenario`, in full: [One call, end to end](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd). - A grid of campaigns rather than a list: [A scenario grid](../06-scenarios/scenario-grid.qmd).
